title: Kiran Arora vs Laxma Dass on 25 September, 2025
full_text: Kiran Arora vs Laxma Dass on 25 September, 2025 IN THE COURT OF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS-02, DISTRICT EAST, KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI Presided by: Ms. Neha Garg, DJS CNR NO. DLET020070402020 CT CASE No. 2444/2020 KIRAN ARORA VS. LAXMAN DASS 1.) Name of the Complainant : KIRAN ARORA W/o Sh. Manoj Arora, R/o 12/125, Geeta Colony, Delhi-110031. 2.) Name of the accused : LAXMAN DASS and parentage S/o Not known, R/o 117, Gali No. 4, New Lahore, Shastri Nagar, Geeta Colony, Delhi-110031. 3.) Offence complained of : u/s. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 . 4.) Plea of accused persons : Pleaded not guilty 5.) Date of institution of the case : 01.10.2020 6.) Final order : ACQUITTAL 7.) Reserved for judgment on : 25.09.2025 CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 1 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 8.) Judgment pronounced on : 25.09.2025 JUDGMENT 01.By way of the present Judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by Kiran Arora (hereinafter referred to as 'complainant') against Laxman Dass (hereinafter referred to as 'accused') u/s. 138 r/w s. 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as 'the NI Act ') for dishonor of cheque bearing no. 738157 dated 28.07.2020 amounting to ₹2,00,000/- drawn on State Bank of India, Geeta Colony, Delhi (hereinafter referred to as 'the cheque in question'). BRIEF FACTUAL MATRIX OF THE PRESENT CASE: - 02.Succinctly put, it is the case of complainant that he and the accused was having friendly relations with complainant's husband. It is stated that the accused approached the complainant for a friendly loan of ₹2,00,000/-, in March 2019, with an assurance to repay the same within a period of one year. Based on prior relations with the accused and repeated assurances, the complainant disbursed ₹2,00,000/- to the accused on 29.03.2019, who issued the cheque in question. 03.It is stated in the complaint that the cheque in question issued by the accused was deposited by the complainant in her bank i.e., Central Bank of India, Branch Patparganj Road, Delhi and the same was returned dishonored with the remarks 'Payments stopped by the drawers' on 31.07.2020. CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 2 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 04.It is further stated that complainant contacted the accused and disclosed about the dishonour of cheque in question and demanded the amount of the cheque in cash, but at that time, accused started bargaining for time on one pretext or the other but did not pay the same. Consequently, the complainant sent a legal notice dated 13.08.2020 u/s. 138 of the NI Act to the addresses of accused by his counsel through speed post vide postal receipt but despite the service of the legal notice, the accused had neither made the payments of the above said cheque nor had replied to the said notice. Hence, the present complaint. PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE COURT: - 05.The cognizance of the complainant was taken and accused was summoned vide Order dated 09.10.2020. Notice u/s. 251 of Cr.P.C. was served upon the accused persons on 28.04.2023 to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Thereafter, the case was fixed for complainant evidence. 06.Thereafter, complainant examined himself as CW-1 in support of his case. CW-1 was examined, cross-examined and discharged and thereafter, complainant evidence was closed on 16.09.2025 and statement of accused u/s. 313 of Cr.P.C. was recorded separately on 16.09.2025, wherein accused Laxman Dass has stated that he knows the complainant and her husband but he had not taken a loan of ₹2,00,000/- from the complainant on 29.03.2019. Accused has stated that he had to return CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 3 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:13 +0530 ₹95,000/- to the husband of the complainant on account of his borrowing made from the complainant's husband at different times and out of the said amount, he had already repaid ₹37,000/- to the husband of the complainant. Accused has further stated that he had given one blank signed cheque to the husband of the complainant in the year 2018-19, which has been misused by the complainant by filing the present case. Accused has stated that has no liability towards the complainant for the amount of the cheque in question. Accused has further stated that he had not received the said legal notice. 07.Thereafter, the matter was listed for defence evidence. Accused had moved an application u/s. 315 of Cr.P.C to examine himself in his defence and the same was allowed by the Court. Thereafter, accused examined himself as DW1 in his defence and he was also cross- examined and discharged and DE was closed vide order dated 17.09.2025 and the matter was fixed for final arguments. 08.I have heard both the Counsels at length. I have considered the evidence led by both the parties carefully and have perused the Court record thoroughly. LAW UNDER CONSIDERATION: - 09.Before adverting to the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides. In order to establish the offence u/s. 138 of the NI Act, the complainant must fulfill CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 4 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 all the essential ingredients of the offence, as highlighted below: 1st Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by a person on an account maintained by him/her for payment of money and the same is presented for payment within a period of 3 months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity; 2nd Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by the drawer for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability; 3rd Ingredient: The cheque was returned unpaid by the bank due to either insufficiency of funds in the account to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account on an agreement made with that bank; 4th Ingredient: A demand of the said amount has been made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque by a notice in writing given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information of the dishonour of cheque from the bank; 5th Ingredient: The drawer fails to make payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days from the date of receipt of notice. 10.Once the ingredients mentioned in the foregoing paragraph are established by the complainant, then as soon as the execution of impugned cheque is admitted by the accused, a factual base is established to invoke the presumption of cheque having been issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability by virtue of Section 118(a) CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 5 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 read with Section 139 of NI Act. This is a reverse onus clause, which means that unless the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that the impugned cheque was drawn by the accused for a consideration and that the complainant had received it in discharge of a debt/ liability from the accused. In the case titled as Bir Singh vs. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197, it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that once the accused has admitted the signature on the cheque in question, then the court is bound to raise presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. 11.It has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the judgment titled Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE COUNSELS: - 12.Ld. Counsel for the complainant has submitted that the accused should be convicted of offence punishable u/s. 138 of the NI Act because the CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 6 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 complainant has proved the original cheque, which the accused has not disputed as being drawn on his account. He has further submitted that the cheque in question was returned unpaid vide cheque returning memo which is on record. The same is also not disputed by accused. He has further submitted that the legal demand notice was sent to accused on his admitted address and is proved by postal receipts and the tracking report. He has further submitted that the fact that the payment was not made within 15 days of the receipt of the legal notice is also not disputed. Ld. Counsel for complainant has further submitted that the defence of accused is palpably false as on one hand it has been suggested to the complainant in his cross-examination that the accused had returned ₹75,000/- to the complainant whereas on the other hand, the accused has deposed before the court that he had returned a sum of ₹37,000/- to the complainant. Ld. Counsel for complainant has further submitted that document Ex.CW1/D1 is forged and fabricated as the son of the complainant had met with an accident and passed away on 20.03.2020 and therefore, the complainant could not have given any receiving as shown at point 'D' in the said document. 13.Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the accused has submitted that the accused never received the legal demand notice and that there is no legally enforceable debt or liability of the accused persons towards the complainant to the tune of the amount of the cheque in question as the cheque in question were actually handed over as security cheques to the CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 7 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:13 +0530 husband of the complainant in the year 2018-2019 in blank signed form. Ld. counsel for accused has submitted that the accused had to return ₹95,000/- to the husband of the complainant and out of the said amount, the accused had repaid ₹37,000/- and the complainant and her son had also given acknowledgment(s) of the amount repaid vide document Ex. CW1/D1. Ld. Counsel for accused has submitted that due to typographical error, an amount of ₹75,000/- has been mentioned in the cross-examination of complainant dated 21.04.2025. REASONS FOR THE DECISION: - 14.In the present case, in order to discharge the initial burden to prove the above-mentioned ingredients, complainant has relied upon his evidence affidavit being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record several documents being Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/4. Accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question. Accordingly, this Court raises presumption under Section 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act that the cheque in question was issued by the accused to the complainant in discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability. In order to rebut the presumption, the burden of proof shifts to the accused to prove on a preponderance of probabilities that there was no liability for the amount of the cheque in question. Therefore, in the present matter, the onus of proof is now upon the accused to raise a probable defence and to rebut the presumption of the existence of a legally recoverable debt arisen in favour of the complainant. Now I shall be discussing in detail the defences of the CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 8 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 accused. DEFENCE THAT THE ACCUSED HAS NOT RECEIVED THE LEGAL DEMAND NOTICE: - 15.It is the defense of the accused that he didn't receive the legal demand notice. It is pertinent to note here that the accused has admitted his address mentioned on the legal demand notice in his statement recorded u/s. 313 of Cr.P.C . The complainant has placed on record the postal receipt to prove the deemed service of legal demand notice upon the admitted addresses of accused. Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 and Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 gives a combine effect that the legal demand notice sent through registered post to the correct address is deemed served on that address in the due course of time unless the contrary is proved. 16.Moreover, it was held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decision cited as C.C. Alavi Haji vs. Palapetty Muhammed &Anr. (2007) 6 SCC 555 that a person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. 17.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has very well discussed this defence CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 9 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 in K. Bhaskaran vs. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan and Anr. (1999) 7 SCC 510, where it was held that if a strict interpretation is given that the drawer should have actually received the notice for the period of 15 days to start running no matter that the payee sent the notice on the correct address, a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by different strategies and he could escape from the legal consequences of Section 138 of the NI Act. Thus, for the detailed reasons aforementioned, the plea of the accused that the legal demand notice was never received is not tenable and accordingly, the same is rejected. DEFENCE THAT THERE IS NO LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE DEBT/LIABILITY: - 18.It is the defence of the accused that he has no liability towards the complainant to the tune of the amount of the cheque in question as he had to only return ₹95,000/- to the husband of the complainant, out of which he had already returned ₹37,000/- to the husband of the complainant. 19.Before proceeding to decide the merits of the present defence raised by the accused, it is pertinent to note that in order to rebut the presumption of Section 139 of the NI Act, the accused is not required to bring direct evidence but should adduce sufficient cogent evidence or can rely upon the circumstances which shows the probability of non-existence of consideration. Accused has to prove his defence only on the scale of preponderance of possibilities as has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 10 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 Court in the case of Basalingappa vs. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418. 20.The defence under consideration requires a conscientious consideration of the cross-examination of the complainant. Complainant has deposed in her cross-examination that she is a home maker and her husband, daughter and son were working and she had some money from which the loan was advanced to the accused. Complainant had deposed that the amount of ₹2,00,000/- was given in cash to the accused out of which ₹1,00,000/- was kept with her and the remaining amount of ₹1,00,000/- was withdrawn by her from her bank account. Complainant has further deposed that she cannot produce the bank account statement of the account from which she has withdrawn ₹1,00,000/- as the said account belonged to her deceased son. She has further deposed that she has advanced the loan amount to the accused in the presence of her husband, daughter and son and that no written agreement was executed with the accused with respect to the loan transaction. Complainant has denied the suggestion that she had given receiving at point A, B, C and D of document Ex. CW1/D1 to the accused. She has further denied the suggestion that the accused had to only return ₹95,000/- out of which the accused had already returned ₹37,000/- on different dates. 21.It becomes clear from the aforesaid cited testimony of the complainant that no written agreement or promissory note was executed for the present loan. However, as per the testimony of the complainant, she has CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 11 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 advanced the loan amount to the accused in the presence of her husband, daughter and son. It is pertinent to note here that the complainant has failed to examine her husband and daughter in support of her case. No reasonable prudent person would advance any such amount in cash to any person without executing any written document especially when the lender does not have any independent income. The aforesaid conduct of the complainant is contrary to the ordinary human conduct. This testimony of complainant and her inability to examine her husband and her daughter raises serious doubt about the advancing of the loan in the first instance. In Vijay vs. Laxman & Anr. (2013) 3 SCC 86, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed: - "The absence of any details of the date on which the loan was advanced as also the absence of any documen- tary or other evidence to show that any such loan trans- action had indeed taken place between the parties is a significant circumstance." 22.At this stage, it is imperative to note the settled position of law that in case of cash transactions, showcasing that complainant did not have adequate financial capacity and sources of funds to lend money to the accused amounts to a probable defense and can help in rebutting the presumption that accrued to the benefit of the complainant in cheque dishonor cases. The relevant case laws in this regard have been reproduced hereunder for reference. 23.In Rajaram (since deceased) through LRs. vs. Maruthachalam (since CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 12 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 deceased) Through LRs. Criminal appeal no. 1978 of 2013 decided on January 18, 2023 by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, the acquittal of the accused by the trial court was upheld by Apex Court and it was held that the agricultural income was not shown by the complainant in his Income Tax Returns and from the income shown in the ITR, it is proved that the complainant didn't have the financial capacity to lend ₹3,00,000/- to the accused. 24.In Tedhi Singh vs. Narayan Dass Mahant (2022) 6 SCC 73, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that it cannot be expected of the complainant to initially lead evidence to show that he had the financial capacity. However, the accused has the right to demonstrate that the complainant in a particular case did not have the financial capacity to lend the loan. The same can be done by accused by producing independent materials, namely, by examining his witnesses and producing documents, by pointing to the materials produced by the complainant himself, or through the cross examination of the witnesses of the complainant. 25.In Prem Singh Rohila vs. State of Haryana and Anr. , decided by Hon'ble Punjab and Haryana High Court on 2 March, 2022 the conviction of trial court and session court was overruled by Hon'ble High Court and the accused was acquitted as the complainant failed to prove his financial capacity. It was held as follows: CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 13 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 "20. A perusal of the same shows that the failure of the complainant to display his financial capacity to advance the amount alleged to have been lent would shift the burden on the complainant to prove his financial capacity to lend the money as well as the other circumstances to establish existence of consideration for issuance of cheque. After noticing that there was no evidence led before the Court to indicate the financial capacity of the complainant to lend the money in question, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the judgment of conviction suffered perversity and was thus liable to be set aside. It was observed that the accused had raised a probable defence and that the complainant failed to prove his financial capacity on the basis of evidence led by him and thus ordered acquittal of the accused." (Emphasis supplied) 26.In John. K. Abraham vs. Simon C. Abraham and Ors. in Crmnl. Appeal 2043 of 2013 decided on 05.12.2013 in which it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that: "It has to be stated that in order to draw the presumption under Section 118 read along with 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act , the burden was heavily upon the complainant to have shown that he had required funds for having advanced the money to the accused; that the issuance of the cheque in support of the said payment advanced was true and that the accused was bound to make the payment as had been agreed while issuing the cheque in favor of the complainant." (Emphasis laid) CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 14 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 27.In K. Prakashan vs. P.K. Surenderan (2007 (4) CCC 713 SC) the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that the Complainant is required to show his solvency to the extent of the loan either through the bank account or through other means. 28.In Basalingappa vs. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as follows: "During his cross-examination, when financial capacity to pay ₹6 lakhs to the accused was questioned, there was no satisfactory reply given by the complainant. The evidence on record, thus, is a probable defence on behalf of the accused, which shifted the burden on the complainant to prove his financial capacity and other facts." (Emphasis laid) 29.In APS Forex Service Private Limited vs. Shakti International Fashion Linkers AIR 2020 SC 945, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has clarified and explained the issue as follows: "We are of the view that whenever the accused has questioned the financial capacity of the complainant in support of his probable defence, despite the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act about the presumption of legally enforceable debt and such presumption is rebuttable, thereafter the onus shifts again on the complainant to prove his financial capacity and at that stage the complainant is required to lead the evidence to prove his financial capacity, more CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 15 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 particularly when it is a case of giving loan by cash and thereafter issuance of a cheque." (Emphasis added) 30.The crux of the aforesaid decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court has been summarized by the Hon'ble Kerala High Court in Sunitha vs. Sheela Antony , 2020 SCC OnLine Ker 1750 In my view, the crux of the decisions referred to above is the following: "The complainant has no obligation, in all cases under Section 138 of the Act, to prove his financial capacity. But, when the case of the complainant is that he lent money to the accused by cash and that the accused issued the cheque in discharge of the liability, and if the accused challenges the financial capacity of the complainant to advance the money, despite the presumption under Section 139 of the Act, the complainant has the obligation to prove his financial capacity or the source of the money allegedly lent by him to the accused. The complainant has no initial burden to prove his financial capacity or the source of the money. The obligation in that regard would arise only when his capacity or capability to advance the money is challenged by the accused." (Emphasis added) 31.Therefore, the settled law is that in cases in which the underlying debt transaction is a cash transaction, the accused can raise a probable defence by questioning the financial capacity of the complainant as well as the sources of funds to lend the loan, and once the said question is raised, the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity. CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 16 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:13 +0530 32.Therefore, in the present case since the complainant has given alleged loan of ₹2,00,000/- in cash and the financial capacity of the complainant as well as sources of funds to lend the loan in question has been specifically disputed by the accused in the cross-examination of the complainant, thus, the onus is upon the complainant to prove the same. 33.As stated earlier, complainant has deposed in her cross-examination that she had given the amount of ₹2,00,000/- in cash to the accused and that she is a home maker but her husband, daughter and son were working. She has deposed that ₹1,00,000/- was kept with her and the remaining amount of ₹1,00,000/- was withdrawn by her from the bank account of her son and that she cannot produce the statement of the account of the bank from which she has withdrawn ₹1,00,000/- as the said account belonged to her deceased son. 34.Thus, it is to be seen that the complainant has not produced any proof of the sources of her fund. Admittedly, the complainant was not working and therefore, she did not have any independent source of funds. She has vaguely deposed that ₹1,00,000/- was kept with her. She has failed to deposed the source from where she has acquired ₹1,00,000/- which was kept with her and in case she has acquired the same from her husband, daughter and son, she has failed to examine them. Moreover, she has failed to summon the bank account statement of her son from which she CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 17 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 had withdrawn ₹1,00,000/- which was used to advance loan to the accused. The testimony of the complainant that she cannot produce the bank account statement of her deceased son from which she has withdrawn ₹1,00,000/- cannot be accepted as the said statement could have been easily summoned from the concerned bank. The demise of the account holder does not per se put any embargo in proving the bank statement of the account holder. At this stage, I would be remiss to mention that complainant has also materially contradicted herself about the sources of funds as it is stated in para 3 of the complaint that she has advanced the loan from "her account" and from her savings whereas she has deposed before the Court that the amount of ₹1,00,000/- was withdrawn by her from her bank account of her son. The aforesaid material contradiction further casts doubt on the sources of funds of the complainant to lend the alleged amount. Hence the source of funds ₹2,00,000/- by the complainant remains not proved. 35.Thus, the failure of the complainant to bring any documentary proof of the alleged loan transaction, her failure to examine her husband & her daughter in support of her case and her failure to adequately depose about & prove her sources of funds, has resulted in the rebuttal of the mandatory presumption existing in favour of the complainant. Onus is now on the complainant to prove the alleged loan transaction of ₹2,00,000/-. CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 18 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 36.Ld. Counsel for the complainant has argued that the defence of the accused is false as on one hand it has been suggested to the complainant in his cross-examination that the accused had returned ₹75,000/- to the complainant whereas on the other hand, the accused has deposed before the court that he had returned a sum of ₹37,000/- to the complainant. Ld. Counsel for complainant has further submitted that document Ex.CW1/D1 is forged and fabricated as the son of the complainant had met with an accident and passed away on 20.03.2020 and therefore, the complainant could not have given any receiving as shown at point 'D' in document Ex.CW1/D1. 37.Per contra, Ld. Counsel for accused has submitted that due to typographical error, an amount of ₹75,000/- has been mentioned in the cross-examination of complainant dated 21.04.2025. Also, accused has denied in his cross-examination that the son of the complainant had passed away on 20.03.2020 and the complainant and her husband had rushed to hospital to look after their son and therefore, there was no occasion for the complainant to give receiving at point 'D' on document Ex. CW1/D1. Be that as may, is is a settled principle of law that the case of the complainant has to stand on its own legs and that it cannot derive any strength from the weakness of the defence. In the instant case, it is to be seen that the case of the complainant is inherently very weak. The inability of the complainant to bring any documentary proof of the alleged loan transaction, her failure to examine her husband & her CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 19 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:15 +0530 daughter in support of her case and her failure to adequately depose about & prove her sources of funds, casts a doubt on the case of complainant. There is also inconsistency and contradiction in the case of the complainant as projected in para 3 of the complaint and her deposition in the cross examination as noted above. Apart from the cheque in question, there is no other evidence produced by the complainant to substantiate the advancement of loan to the accused. 38.As stated earlier, the accused can prove his defence by drawing inferences from the materials already on record (including complainant's evidences), circumstances of the case and also leading his own evidence. Therefore, without going into the veracity of the testimony of defence set up by the accused, this Court is of the view that the accused by cross- examining the complainant have been able to rebut the mandatory presumption existing in favour of the complainant. It is imperative to understand that in order to pronounce a conviction in a criminal case, the accused 'must be' guilty and not merely ' may be' guilty. For an accused to be guilty, guilt should not be based on mere surmises and conjectures but it should be based on cogent evidence. The accused has clearly presented a defence that appears probable and as per the settled law, this is all that is required as preponderance of probabilities is not a rigorous standard of proof, but only so much evidence as makes the Court lean in favour of one side and not the other. Consequently, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused. CT Case No. 2444/2020 Kiran Arora vs. Laxman Dass Page No. 20 of 21 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA Date: GARG GARG 2025.09.25 15:59:14 +0530 39.In view of the aforesaid findings and analysis, this Court has arrived at the irresistible conclusion that the no offence u/s. 138 of the NI Act is made out against the accused as the accused has been able to cast a shadow of reasonable doubt upon the case of the complainant by rebutting the mandatory presumption resting in favour of the complainant. Complainant has utterly failed to prove her case beyond reasonable doubt qua the existence of liability of the accused on the date of the drawl or presentation of the cheque in question. Since the basic ingredient which is pivotal to attract liability under Section 138 of the NI Act has not been proved by the complainant, accordingly no offence of dishonour of the cheque in question under the said Section is made out. FINAL ORDER: - 40.Accordingly, accused Laxman Dass is hereby acquitted from the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Announced in the open Court (NEHA GARG) on 25.09.2025 JMFC-02, East District, KKD Courts, Delhi Note: This judgment contains 21 pages and each page has been signed by me.
